instructions:
Below is a draft essay. Revise it so that it reads as if a US grade 8 student wrote it in class for a timed writing test. Keep the position it argues and keep it at about 161 words. The file must contain only the revised essay.

A measurement tool scored the draft on how it carries feeling. For each measure below it gives the current value and a target. Revise the essay so that its measures move to the targets; the tool will score the result again.
- positive charge (hedons per 1,000 words): now 123.0, target 85.5. Counts positive words such as good, love, fun.
- negative charge (dolors per 1,000 words): now 8.4, target 6.4. Counts negative words such as bad, hate, problem.
- words that carry charge (% of words): now 34.4, target 26.4. Counts share of all words that carry any feeling.
- charge under a negation (% of charge): now 6.4, target 3.1. Counts feeling words placed under not, never or n't.
- charge after an intensifier such as 'very' (% of charge): now 0.0, target 2.3. Counts feeling words placed right after very, really or so.
- charge after a contrast word such as 'but' (% of charge): now 0.0, target 8.2. Counts feeling words placed after but or however in the same sentence.
- net charge of the last fifth minus the text's mean (per 1,000 words): now 83.5, target -0.9. Counts how much more positive the last fifth is than the essay as a whole; negative means a more downbeat ending.
- how unevenly charge is spread over sentences (1 = as if words were dealt at random): now 2.3, target 0.8. Counts above 1 means the feeling is bunched into some sentences while others are plain; below 1 means it is spread evenly.

Draft:

Dear Principal,

I am writing to ask you to choose Policy 1, which lets students bring phones to school and use them at lunch and during free periods, provided they stay off in class.

My main reason is safety. Many of us walk home, take the bus, or stay late for practice, and our parents need a way to reach us when plans change. A phone left at home cannot help a student whose ride never shows up.

Second, Policy 1 teaches responsibility. Learning when to put a phone away is a skill we will need at every job we ever hold. A total ban only postpones that lesson.

Finally, Policy 2 would be hard to enforce. Teachers would spend their time searching backpacks instead of teaching, and students would simply hide their phones.

Policy 1 protects class time while trusting students during their own time. I hope you will give us the chance to earn that trust.

Sincerely,
A Student
